desc:
Given an m x n integer matrix and an integer k, consider every non-empty rectangle of consecutive rows and consecutive columns. Return the largest sum of the cells of a rectangle whose sum is at most k.

The input guarantees that at least one rectangle has a sum that does not exceed k, so the answer always exists. The matrix may contain negative numbers.
constraints: At least one rectangle has a sum that is at most k
hints: Enumerating all rectangles with a 2-D prefix sum is O(m²n²). Reduce the problem to one dimension: fix the top and bottom row.
For a fixed pair of rows, add the rows column by column to get a 1-D array of column sums. You need the best subarray sum that is at most k in that array.

With prefix sums P of the 1-D array, a subarray ending at j has sum P[j] - P[i]. To make it as large as possible while ≤ k you need the smallest earlier prefix that is ≥ P[j] - k: a lower-bound query on a sorted list of earlier prefixes.
editorial: Choose the thinner dimension as the 'column' side by transposing when needed (here m ≤ n is not required for correctness, only for speed). For every pair of rows (top, bottom) maintain the array col[c] = sum of column c between those rows. The best rectangle with these rows is the best subarray of col with sum ≤ k.

Scan col with a running prefix sum P and a sorted list seen of the earlier prefixes (initially [0]). The subarray ending here that starts after an earlier prefix q has sum P - q. It is ≤ k exactly when q ≥ P - k, and it is maximal for the smallest such q. The lower bound bisect_left(seen, P - k) finds that q (if the index is inside the list), then insert P into seen to keep it sorted.

The cost is O(m² · n log n) when the loop over row pairs is on the smaller dimension. Inserting into a Python list is O(n) in the worst case but very fast in practice for n ≤ 60. A common shortcut: if you find a sum exactly equal to k you can stop, since nothing larger is allowed.
